title: Epidemiology
sentences: Epidemiology is the study of diseases and disorders in a human population.
It is a cornerstone of public health, and shapes policy decisions and evidence-based practice by identifying risk factors for disease and targets for preventive healthcare.
Epidemiologists help with study design, collection, and statistical analysis of data, amend interpretation and dissemination of results (including peer review and occasional systematic review).
Epidemiology has helped develop methodology used in clinical research, public health studies, and, to a lesser extent, basic research in the biological sciences.

Major areas of epidemiological study include disease causation, transmission, outbreak investigation, disease surveillance, environmental epidemiology, forensic epidemiology, occupational epidemiology, screening, biomonitoring, and comparisons of treatment effects such as in clinical trials.

Epidemiologists rely on other scientific disciplines like biology to better understand disease processes, statistics to make efficient use of the data and draw appropriate conclusions, social sciences to better understand proximate and distal causes, and engineering for exposure assessment.
Epidemiology, literally meaning 'the study of what is upon the people', is derived from Greek epi 'upon, among', demos 'people' and logos 'study', referring to the study of human populations.

However, the term is widely used in studies of zoological populations (veterinary epidemiology), although the term 'epizootiology' was historically used. 'Epidemiology' has also been applied to studies of plant populations (botanical or plant disease epidemiology).

The distinction between "epidemic" and "endemic" was first drawn by Hippocrates, The term "epidemiology" appears to have first been used to describe the study of epidemics in 1802 by the Spanish physician Joaquín de Villalba in Epidemiología Española.
Before the 1800s, however, colonial powers developed the strategies of analysis employed by later Epidemiologists, tracking air and disease in colonial and slave ship environments.
Epidemiologists also study the interaction of diseases in a population, a condition known as a syndemic.

The term epidemiology is now widely applied to cover the description and causation of not only epidemic, infectious disease, but of disease in general, including related conditions and, especially since the 20th century, chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.
Some examples of topics examined through epidemiology include high blood pressure, mental illness and obesity.
Therefore, this epidemiology is based upon how the pattern of the disease causes change in the function of human beings.

The Greek physician Hippocrates, taught by Democritus, was known as the father of medicine, sought a logic to sickness; he is the first person known to have examined the relationships between the occurrence of disease and environmental influences.
Hippocrates believed sickness of the human body to be caused by an imbalance of the four humors (black bile, yellow bile, blood, and phlegm).
The cure to the sickness was to remove or add the humor in question to balance the body.
This belief led to the application of bloodletting and dieting in medicine.
He coined the terms endemic (for diseases usually found in some places but not in others) and epidemic (for diseases that are seen at some times but not others).
The British Empire developed Epidemiological tracking strategies through colonialism.

In the West Indies, the British statistician and general Alexander Tulloch tracked illnesses across the West Indies.Tulloch tracked diseases of the liver, stomach and bowels, brain, heart, and yellow fever.
The diseases are tracked across several locations of colonial interest, such as Jamaica and the Windward and Leeward islands.
In the seventeenth century, the Iberians, while colonizing America, tracked diseases among slave populations.
In Cartagena, Colombia, Crown officials categorized arriving captives according to standards of age, gender, height, health, and disease.
The evaluation of the slaves served tax purposes.
The officials tracked a variety of diseases, including, but not limited to, fevers, dysentery, and syphilis.
Disease also changed the price traders could charge buyers in the colonies, with certain impairments like Asthma incurring greater discount and illnesses like Depression incurring minor discount.
Added up, slaves tracked with multiple physical or mental illnesses could, therefore, be purchased at steep reduction.
Following the Philippine-American war, the United States government instituted steep smallpox mandates.

Due to the high number of smallpox deaths during the war ("conservatively" estimated at 40,000 annually), many Filipinos voluntarily sought vaccination, bringing the reported death count down to 823 after the administering of about 18,000,000 vaccines.
Despite the previous outbreaks, some Filipinos did not voluntarily seek vaccination.
In 1902 Batangas, military units accompanied by physicians would enter houses and vaccinate inhabitants.
Western physicians knew of air's central role to human life before the eighteenth century, but they failed to understand how it could become jeopardized in crowded spaces.
Physicians like the English Robert John Thornton (1768-1837) spent time on slave ships, studying the confined spaces and the environment's affects on captive people.
Thornton describes, after watching one prisoner go without water, the same prisoner growing healthier after being moved to a nearby window.
Thornton concludes that fresh air is necessary to continue life.
Similar to Thornton, Thomas Trotter (1760-1832), described the lack of air on slave ships.
In "Observations on the scurvy," Trotter observes scurvy on one captive person, detailing several symptoms: bloating of the eye, the tongue "locked between the teeth," spongy and bleeding gums.

He identifies the predisposition to scurvy as increasing due to the harsh environments present on slave ships, and that a mixture of nutritional and physical factors made the African captives prone to scurvy.
Vaccination processes have also been affected by colonialism.
In the early nineteenth century, after the creation of the smallpox vaccine, Brazilian physician José Avelino Barbosa traveled to Lisbon, Portugal in 1804, alongside seven enslaved boys.
These seven boys then carried the vaccine back to Bahia, Brazil, in their bodies.

After traveling back to Bahia, the vaccination was transferred via the "arm-to-arm" method—a method where physicians drew pus from the pustules of a vaccinated person, and injected the fluid into an unvaccinated person.
Thus, the enslaved boys became not only the first in Bahia to receive smallpox vaccination, but also an integral part of Bahia's strategy to combat the disease.
Colonial powers developed new epidemiological terminology to understand the spread of disease among their soldiers and captive slaves.
